proof:
# Quantitative uncaptured-fiber thresholds from Doignon

Let C subset R^n x R^d be a convex body with nonempty mixed intersection
S. Use the task's intrinsic dimension q=dim_H S and measure mu=H_q|S.
Let P be the finite set of q-dimensional integer fibers, and put

    K_z=C_z,  w_z=H_q(K_z)>0,  M=sum_(z in P) w_z,
    N=|P|,    W=max_z w_z,     m=2^n.

For q=0 all nonempty fibers are singletons and all w_z=1. Let
H_1,...,H_s be any finite collection of closed ambient halfspaces,
and write

    c_i(z)=H_q(K_z intersect (H_i)_z),
    e_i(z)=w_z-c_i(z)=H_q(K_z minus (H_i)_z).

These are captured and STRICTLY uncaptured masses. A whole intrinsic
fiber on the boundary of a closed cap is captured, not uncaptured.
Suppose mu(H_i)<=B for every i and mB<M.

Define the decreasing continuous function

    F(t)=sum_(z in P) (w_z-t)_+,    0<=t<=W.

If B>0, there is a unique t_* in (0,W) with F(t_*)=mB. For B=0 set
t_*=W. Then an ACTUAL integer fiber z_* satisfies

    e_i(z_*)>=t_* for EVERY i.                           (1)

In particular

    t_*>=(M-mB)/N,
    c_i(z_*)/w_(z_*)<=1-t_*/w_(z_*)<=1-t_*/W.          (2)

This is stronger than saying that each cap has some nonempty remainder
on a common fiber. It is still a statement about INDIVIDUAL remainders:
their intersection inside that fiber is not claimed nonempty.

## 1. Integer convexity of absolute remainder thresholds

For t>0 put Q_i(t)={z in P:e_i(z)>=t}. Then

    conv(Q_i(t)) intersect Z^n=Q_i(t).                  (3)

For q>=1, take a representation z=sum_l alpha_l z_l with positive
coefficients summing to one and z_l in Q_i(t). Each strict-negative
remainder in K_(z_l) has positive q-volume, so it contains compact
convex subsets with q-volumes tending to e_i(z_l). Their Minkowski
average lies in K_z and remains strictly outside H_i by affinity.
Its affine dimension is at least q. It is at most q because z is
integer and q is the maximum dimension of all integer fibers.

Consequently all source direction spaces in this representation
coincide with one q-dimensional space: the direction space of a
Minkowski sum is the sum of the source direction spaces, each of
dimension q. After translating within this common space, ordinary
q-dimensional Brunn--Minkowski applies with the standard H_q
normalization. Passing to the compact-subset limits gives

    e_i(z)^(1/q)>=sum_l alpha_l e_i(z_l)^(1/q)>=t^(1/q).

This proves (3), while also showing that z belongs to P. Such compact
inner approximants can be obtained by imposing a small strictly
negative margin and a small relative-interior erosion; their volumes
increase to the remainder's volume. No boundary mass is moved to the
wrong side of the cap.

For q=0 the remainders are singleton points or empty. If Q_i(t) is
nonempty then t<=1. Averaging its strictly negative points at an
integer base supplies a strictly negative point in K_z, which is a
singleton by maximality of q. This proves (3) in the counting case.

The same dimension argument without cap remainders proves
conv(P) intersect Z^n=P. Empty Q_i(t) are permitted, with empty convex
hull. Vertical caps and caps constant on an intrinsic affine fiber
are included by the strict-negative-margin argument.

## 2. Quantitative Doignon proof

If B=0, every cap has zero mass on every positive fiber, so any
maximum-volume fiber satisfies (1). Assume B>0. Suppose the sets
Q_i(t_*) have empty intersection. By (3), their convex hulls have
integer-free intersection. Doignon supplies at most m of those
convex hulls with integer-free intersection. For n=0 this is the
direct one-base assertion, requiring no separate theorem.

For every z in P, one of the selected caps therefore has

    e_i(z)<t_*,    hence c_i(z)>w_z-t_*.

Summing selected captured masses over all fibers gives

    sum_selected mu(H_i)>sum_z(w_z-t_*)_+=F(t_*)=mB.

The strict sign is justified because F(t_*)=mB>0, so at least one
fiber has w_z>t_*. Contributions from all other fibers are nonnegative.
The selected family has at most m members of mass at most B, a
contradiction. This proves (1). Finally F(t)>=M-Nt gives the first
inequality in (2); the remaining ones are immediate.

## 3. A genuinely partial cut when the family covers S

Assume now the caps cover S. For q>=1 let g be the ordinary intrinsic
centroid of K_(z_*). At least one original cap, say H_j, contains
(z_*,g). Grünbaum inside the q-dimensional affine hull gives

    c_j(z_*)>=gamma_q w_(z_*),
    e_j(z_*)>=t_*,                                       (4)

where gamma_q=(q/(q+1))^q. Since t_*>0, this cap cannot contain the
whole affine fiber; its restriction is a proper intrinsic halfspace.
Thus (4) is an ACTUAL substantial partial slice, with exact lower
bounds on both sides. In particular

    w_(z_*)>=t_*/(1-gamma_q),
    c_j(z_*)>=gamma_q t_*/(1-gamma_q).                    (5)

No common point outside all caps has been inferred from (1). The
centroid argument uses coverage of the fiber, not an intersection
of its individual remainders.

Under the task's hypothesized budget B<gamma_d M/m and q>=1,

    t_*>(1-gamma_d)M/N.

Every cap misses at least this absolute amount on the SAME fiber,
and (4) selects one proper cap that also captures at least gamma_q
of that fiber. This quantitative conclusion depends on the actual
volume distribution and does not resolve OC.

For q=0, every e_i(z_*)>=t_*>0 means every cap misses that singleton.
This contradicts a cover. Thus in this case every finite cap cover
has a cap of mass at least M/m, as in the usual counting Doignon bound.

## 4. An explicit volume-distribution lower bound for cap covers

For all q>=0, with gamma_0=1, any finite closed cap cover satisfies

    max_i mu(H_i)
      >= (1/m) sum_(z in P) [w_z-(1-gamma_q)W]_+.        (6)

If B=max_i mu(H_i)>=M/m this is immediate. Otherwise Sections 2-3
apply; (5) gives t_*<=(1-gamma_q)W. Since F is decreasing,
mB=F(t_*)>=F((1-gamma_q)W), proving (6). The counting case was
handled directly above and gives the same formula.

Equal-volume fibers give the exact value gamma_q M/m on the right.
More generally, if all w_z>=(1-epsilon)W with 0<=epsilon<gamma_q,
(6) gives

    max_i mu(H_i)/M
      >=(gamma_q-epsilon)/[m(1-epsilon)].               (7)

Indeed all summands in (6) are positive, so their sum is
M-N(1-gamma_q)W, and NW/M<=1/(1-epsilon). Formula (6) also counts
every fiber with w_z>(1-gamma_q)W, not only the maximum-volume ones.
These are finite-cover bounds. An exact critical-cover theorem may
convert them to center-depth bounds, but no such conversion or
general sharp mixed constant is assumed in this proof.

There is also an exact implicit budget bound, obtained by retaining
the fact that the centroid-containing cap in (4) has TOTAL mass at
most B. It gives w_(z_*)<=B/gamma_q, hence
t_*<=[(1-gamma_q)/gamma_q]B. Therefore every finite cap cover obeys

    sum_z [w_z-((1-gamma_q)/gamma_q)B]_+ <= mB.          (7a)

If mB>=M this is immediate; otherwise it follows from monotonicity
of F and the displayed bound on t_*. For q=0 it reads M<=mB and
was already proved. For N equal weights, (7a) yields

    B >= M/[m+N(1-gamma_q)/gamma_q].

When N>=m this improves the elementary single-heavy-fiber estimate
gamma_q M/N. It remains weaker than (6) in that equal-weight case;
no improvement over every previously available bound is asserted.

## 5. Convex root thresholds retain more finite data

For q>=1, let ell be convex on conv(P) and positive on P. Its
superlevel comparison sets

    Q_i(ell)={z in P:e_i(z)^(1/q)>=ell(z)}

are lattice-convex. Indeed, at an integer convex combination the
uncaptured-volume root is at least the weighted sum of source roots,
which is at least the weighted sum of ell values, which in turn is
at least ell at the target by convexity. This is the same dimension-
tracked Brunn--Minkowski argument as in Section 1.

If ell(z)^q>(1-gamma_q)w_z for every z, these sets have empty common
intersection: at a common fiber every cap would capture strictly
less than gamma_q w_z, contradicting coverage of its centroid.
Doignon and the same captured-mass sum therefore give

    sum_z [w_z-ell(z)^q]_+ <= mB.                       (7b)

The conclusion also holds under non-strict ell(z)^q>=(1-gamma_q)w_z:
first replace ell by (1+epsilon)ell and then pass to the limit in
the finite sum. No common uncovered point is inferred.

Equivalently, let ell be convex on conv(P) and suppose

    ell(z)>=w_z^(1/q) for all z in P.

Then every finite cap cover satisfies the additional bound

    max_i mu(H_i)
      >=(1/m) sum_z [w_z-(1-gamma_q)ell(z)^q]_+.         (8)

To prove it, assume the contrary and choose eta>0 small enough that
eta<gamma_q and

    mB<sum_z[w_z-(1-gamma_q+eta)ell(z)^q]_+.

The sets

    Q_i={z:e_i(z)^(1/q)>=(1-gamma_q+eta)^(1/q)ell(z)}

are lattice-convex by the argument above, and ell is positive on P. If their
intersection were empty, the same Doignon selection and fiber sum
would contradict the displayed strict inequality. Thus some z
belongs to all Q_i. At this fiber every cap captures at most

    w_z-(1-gamma_q+eta)ell(z)^q
       <=(gamma_q-eta)w_z,

contradicting coverage of its centroid and intrinsic Grünbaum.
This proves (8). Constant ell=W^(1/q) recovers (6). Affine majorants
are an important permitted special case. Contact fibers
where ell(z)=w_z^(1/q) contribute exactly gamma_q w_z, while some
noncontact fibers also give positive contributions. A single such
majorant need not control all source mass.

## 6. Relative-fraction thresholds are not integer convex

The absolute-threshold mechanism cannot be replaced by an assumed
integer convexity of {z:e_i(z)>=theta w_z}. An exact n=d=1 example is

    C={-1<=z<=1, 3|z|-3<=x<=1},
    H={x<=0}.

The three integer fibers have lengths (1,4,1), and their strict
uncaptured lengths are (1,1,1). At theta=1/2 the qualifying bases
are {-1,1}, while their integer midpoint 0 does not qualify. The
body is compact, convex and full dimensional; the cap is closed
and nonvertical. Taking a product with a unit-volume continuous
cube gives the same obstruction for every d>=1.

This is an obstruction to the relative-superlevel-set assertion,
not an OC counterexample. The quantitative conclusions above retain
absolute remainder masses or convex ROOT thresholds, precisely the
forms for which integer convexity has been proved.
